Answer ALL the 50 questions in this examination; all questions carry equal marks. Non-programmable calculators are allowed. Each question has FOUR suggested answers A, B, C and D: decide which answer is appropriate and mark only one answer for each question (if you mark more than one answer you score zero for that question). Use a soft HB pencil, avoid spending too much time on any one question, and do all rough work in the booklet. Mobile phones are not allowed in the examination room.

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the European nation whose missionaries were the first to open schools and mission stations at the coast of Cameroon in the 1850s.
questions.corrige_markdown: The pioneers on the Cameroon coast were British Baptist missionaries of the Baptist Missionary Society (Joseph Merrick at Bimbia from the 1840s, then Alfred Saker at Douala and, in 1858, at Victoria). They opened the first mission stations and schools. German missionaries (the Basel Mission, from 1886) only arrived after the German annexation of 1884, France had no mission on this coast in the 1850s, and Portugal had left only traders' contacts and a few names (such as Rio dos Camaroes). **Answer: A.**
themes: christian missions on the cameroon coast

questions.enonce_markdown: The agent of the Karl Woermann Trading firm in Douala who was very instrumental in negotiating German annexation of Cameroon was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Johannes Voss, a German trading agent at Douala (presented in the usual Cameroonian textbook accounts as the Woermann agent), negotiated with the Douala chiefs (Bell and Akwa) and prepared the treaty signed on 12 July 1884 (the Germano-Douala Treaty). Gustav Nachtigal was not a firm's agent: he was the Imperial Commissioner who arrived on the gunboat Moewe and proclaimed the German protectorate over the coast in July 1884. The other names are not the Douala agent credited with this role in the standard accounts. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Max Buchner is important in the history of German administration of Cameroon because he ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Max Buchner, a German explorer and doctor, was in Douala in 1884-1885 and is remembered as the first German imperial representative (acting imperial official) on the spot, at the start of German rule. The special envoy sent to annex the coast, who also came on the Moewe, was Gustav Nachtigal, so options B and C describe Nachtigal and not Buchner. Option A does not describe any act of Buchner. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: was special German envoy to annex Cameroon
brought the Moewe to the coast of Cameroon
was first German Imperial Representative to Cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the group of British nationals at the coast of Cameroon associated with the Scramble for Cameroon in 1884.
questions.corrige_markdown: The British people at the coast linked to the Scramble for Cameroon are Consul Edward Hewett, who arrived in July 1884 a few days after Nachtigal had already obtained the treaties for Germany, and the Baptist missionaries Alfred Saker and Joseph Merrick, who had long urged Britain to annex the coast. Gladstone (Prime Minister) and Queen Victoria were in London and did not answer the Douala petitions in time, and the other names do not form the group usually cited. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The annexation of Cameroon in 1884 was formalised by ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Cameroon became a German protectorate through the Germano-Douala Treaty signed on 12 July 1884 between the Douala chiefs (Bell and Akwa) and the agents of the German firms (Woermann and Jantzen and Thormaehlen), then confirmed by Nachtigal. The Berlin Act of 1885 only set the rules of the partition of Africa (notification and effective occupation); the League of Nations came after the First World War and gave Cameroon to Britain and France as mandates. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In which coastal town did the Germans establish the first primary School in Cameroon.
questions.corrige_markdown: Douala, the main trading town and first capital of the German colony, was where the Germans started schooling: the Basel Mission opened schools there from 1886 and the first German government school was opened in Douala about 1887. Victoria had been founded by the British Baptists in 1858, and Tiko and Kribi were not the starting point of German schooling. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The year in which Eugene Zintgraff signed a Blood Pact with the Fon of Bali was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Eugen Zintgraff, the German explorer who opened the Cameroon grasslands for Germany, reached Bali-Nyonga in 1889 and made a blood pact with Fon Galega I, which gave him an ally and a base for his expeditions. The year 1891 is the year of his failed fight against Bafut, not of the pact. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the ethnic resistance against the Germans which led to the death of the German Agent called Conrau.
questions.corrige_markdown: Gustav Conrau, a German explorer and agent who had worked in the grasslands and the Mamfe-Bangwa area, was killed in 1899 in the Bangwa resistance against German penetration. The Bakweri resisted the Germans at the foot of Mount Cameroon (1891) without killing Conrau, and the Nso resistance belongs to another episode of German expansion. **Answer: C.**
themes: indigenous resistance to german rule in cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown:
An important economic achievement under Governor Von Putkamer during German rule in Cameroon was ...

*Options as printed:* A) Creation of Gesseschaft Sud - Kamerun and Gesseschaft Nord West Kamerun   B) Creation of the Botanical Garden in Victoria   C) Construction of Mittelandban (Douala - Edea railway line)   D) Construction of the Nordban (Douala - Nkongsamba railway line)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Jesko von Puttkamer was Governor from 1895 to 1907. His best known economic policy was the grant of huge land and trade concessions to private companies, among them the Gesellschaft Suedkamerun and the Gesellschaft Nordwest Kamerun created in 1898-1899, which opened the way to the plantation and trading economy. The Botanical Garden at Victoria was founded in 1892, before his time as Governor, the Mittelland line (Douala towards Yaounde) was begun in 1908 after he had left, and the Nordbahn (Douala-Nkongsamba) was only started in 1906 and finished in 1911, near the end of his term. Options A and D can both be defended, so the question is left open.

**Intended answer: A (Creation of Gesseschaft Sud - Kamerun and Gesseschaft Nord West Kamerun).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the German Governor whose reign coincided with the defeat and expulsion of the Germans from Cameroon.
questions.corrige_markdown: Karl Ebermaier was Governor from 1912. During his term the Allied (British, French and Belgian) campaign of 1914-1916 ended with the fall of Douala (1914) and Yaounde (1916), and the Germans withdrew into Spanish Guinea in early 1916. Puttkamer (1895-1907), Seitz (1907-1910) and Gleim (1910-1912) had left before the war. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Below is a list of events on the partition of Cameroon. Select the letter that arranges the events in a correct chronological order.

i. League of Nations confirmed Anglo - French partition of Cameroon.

ii. Oliphant - Picot Partition of Cameroon.

iii. Simon - Milner Agreement

iv. Withdrawal of British and French troops to their respective areas.

*Options as printed:* A) i, iv, iii, ii   B) iii, ii, iv, i   C) iv, ii, iii, i   D) ii, iv, ii, i
questions.corrige_markdown:
Order of events: (ii) the Oliphant-Picot partition of March 1916, (iv) the withdrawal of British and French troops to their respective zones, (iii) the Simon-Milner Declaration of July 1919 which fixed the boundary, and (i) the confirmation of the partition by the League of Nations when it granted the mandates in 1922. The correct sequence is ii, iv, iii, i. Option D is printed as "ii, iv, ii, i" (ii repeated, iii missing), which is almost certainly a misprint for ii, iv, iii, i, and no other option is correct, so the question is left open.

**Intended answer: D (ii, iv, ii, i).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.
themes: partition of cameroon after world war one

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the reasons below did NOT influence the British to administer British Cameroons as an integral part of Nigeria?
questions.corrige_markdown: Britain administered the British Cameroons as part of Nigeria for reasons of convenience and economy: the people shared cultures with the neighbouring Nigerian peoples, the territory was poor and could not pay for its own administration, and it was made of two separate strips (a discontinuous territory) lying along the Nigerian border. There is no evidence that the inhabitants asked for this arrangement, so B is the reason that did NOT influence the British. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: The natives requested for this administrative arrangement

questions.enonce_markdown: A prominent traditional ruler from the grass land who represented the Cameroons Province in the Nigeria Eastern House of Assembly under the Richards constitution was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Richards Constitution of 1946 created regional Houses of Assembly in Nigeria, and the Cameroons Province sent representatives to the Eastern House of Assembly at Enugu. Fon Galega II of Bali-Nyonga is the Grassfields ruler usually cited among them. Chief Manga Williams was a coastal chief (Victoria area), not a ruler of the grass land, and the other names are not the Grassfields rulers usually cited for this role. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The leader who spearheaded the Gbaya revolt in 1928 against the French resulting in a series of administrative reforms was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Gbaya revolt (the Kongo-Wara, or 'hoe handle' war) broke out in 1928 in eastern Cameroon and neighbouring territories against French forced labour, recruitment for the Congo-Ocean railway and other exactions. It was led by the Gbaya prophet and healer Karnu (Karno), and it was put down by the French by about 1931, which led to some administrative changes. The other names are not linked to this revolt. **Answer: A.**
themes: revolts in french cameroon under the mandate

questions.enonce_markdown: British Southern Cameroons attained a Quasi-Federal Status in the year ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 gave the Southern Cameroons a quasi-federal status within the Federation of Nigeria, with its own House of Assembly and executive council (E.M.L. Endeley led the government). The year 1947 belongs to the Richards Constitution and 1951 to the Macpherson Constitution, both earlier steps, and 1958 is after the quasi-federal period. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: All the following factors led to the organization of a plebiscite in British Cameroons EXCEPT...
questions.corrige_markdown: The plebiscite was organised under the United Nations because Nigeria was to become independent on 1 October 1960 (so the trusteeship over the British Cameroons had to end), because the Southern Cameroons politicians disagreed on the future (Endeley's side for integration with Nigeria, Foncha's KNDP for reunification), and because the KNDP, in power after the 1959 election, pressed for the question to be settled. The parties in the Southern Cameroons House of Assembly did not hold equal numbers of seats (the KNDP won the 1959 elections), so C is not a factor. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Nigeria was due to gain independence in October 1960
The political parties in the SCHA shared the same number of seats
The KNDP of J.N. Foncha was the ruling party in Southern Cameroons

questions.enonce_markdown: The French Cameroon Prime Minister who in 1958 insisted that French Cameroon was not ripe for Independence was called ...
questions.corrige_markdown: Andre-Marie Mbida, Prime Minister of French Cameroon from 1957, held that the country was not yet ready for independence and resisted the pressure for rapid change; he resigned in February 1958. Ahmadou Ahidjo succeeded him and led the country to independence on 1 January 1960. Um Nyobe was the UPC leader, who demanded immediate independence and reunification and was killed in 1958. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The UPC did not have any seat in the 1956 elections into ALCAM because ...
questions.corrige_markdown: After the riots of May 1955 the French authorities banned the UPC on 13 July 1955, so it could not present candidates in the elections of December 1956 to the Legislative Assembly of Cameroon (ALCAM). Its hostility to some Church leaders and its low support in the North are not the reason for its absence. **Answer: C.**
themes: upc and french repression in cameroon

choix.texte: The UPC was very hostile to the Catholic Church
The party was not popular in the North

questions.enonce_markdown: The reunification between the British Southern Cameroons and the Republic of Cameroon was effected on:
questions.corrige_markdown: Reunification took effect on 1 October 1961, when the Federal Republic of Cameroon was born and the former British Southern Cameroons became West Cameroon. January 1960 is the independence of French Cameroon, February 1961 is the date of the plebiscite, and May 1972 is the referendum that ended the federation. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following economic projects was realised between 1961-1972 to consolidate the unification between West and East Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown: To make unification real, the federal government built links between the two federated states, such as the road between Tiko (West Cameroon) and Douala (East Cameroon). The other projects lie wholly in East Cameroon (the airport and the Douala-Yaounde highway at Douala and Yaounde, and the Yaounde-Ngaoundere railway, completed in the 1970s), so they did not join the two parts of the country. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The Construction of the Douala Airport
The construction of the Yaounde-Ngoundere Railway line.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In what year was the West Cameroon House of Chiefs dissolved ?

*Options as printed:* A) 1961   B) 1965   C) 1966   D) 1972
questions.corrige_markdown:
The West Cameroon House of Chiefs was an institution of the federated state of West Cameroon. It disappeared when the federal structure was ended after the referendum of 20 May 1972, which created the United Republic of Cameroon (the date is the one usually given, but the question is left open because it is not certain).

**Intended answer: D (1972).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The creation of HEVECAM by Ahidjo was aimed at promoting the production of...
questions.corrige_markdown: HEVECAM (Hevea-Cameroun) was created in 1975 under President Ahidjo to produce natural rubber (from the Hevea tree) on large plantations in the south of the country, one of the agro-industrial projects of the 1970s. Palm oil, banana and rice were promoted by other bodies (the CDC, the banana companies, SEMRY). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In 1972, he organized a referendum in the country, dissolved the federal system of government and created the United Republic of Cameroon with Seven Provinces... This statement refers to...
questions.corrige_markdown: President Ahmadou Ahidjo organised the referendum of 20 May 1972 which replaced the federation by a unitary state, the United Republic of Cameroon, divided into seven provinces. Paul Biya changed the name to Republic of Cameroon in 1984, Mbida was Prime Minister in 1957-1958, and Endeley was a Southern Cameroons leader. **Answer: B.**
themes: creation of the united republic of cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown: To fight against corruption in the public service and embezzlement of public funds, the Biya government implemented the following measures EXCEPT...
questions.corrige_markdown: The anti-corruption measures of the Biya government are the anti-corruption units in the ministries and the National Anti-Corruption Commission (CONAC), the imprisonment of embezzlers (for example in the Operation Sparrowhawk of the 2000s) and the Supreme State Audit (CONSUPE), which checks the use of public money. The electoral commission ELECAM (2006) was set up to organise elections, not to fight corruption. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Institution of anti-corruption Units in all ministries (CONAC)
Creation of the Supreme State Audit

questions.enonce_markdown: Cameroon and France share fraternal and diplomatic ties since independence. Identify the International Organisation below in which Cameroon and France have a common membership.
questions.corrige_markdown: Both Cameroon and France are members of the United Nations Organisation (UNO). The African Union and the CEMAC (Central African Economic and Monetary Community) are African bodies that France cannot join, and the Commonwealth, which Cameroon joined in 1995, is made of former British territories and others, but not France. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the motives for the Scramble for Africa listed below was socially beneficial to the Africans?
questions.corrige_markdown: Raw materials, markets for finished goods and the balance of power among European nations were economic and political motives that served Europe. Only the humanitarian motive, the wish to end the slave trade and cruel practices, was a social benefit to Africans. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Need to search for raw materials
Need to balance power among European nations
Need to acquire markets for finished goods
Need to abolish slave trade and inhuman practices.

questions.enonce_markdown: The following were the significance of the battle of Adowa in 1896 in the history of colonisation of Africa EXCEPT...
questions.corrige_markdown: At Adowa (1 March 1896) the army of Emperor Menelik II defeated the Italians, so Ethiopia (Abyssinia) kept its independence and was a symbol of African resistance, and the victory strengthened Menelik's hold on the country. Italy did not colonise Abyssinia as a result of Adowa (it only invaded again in 1935), so C is the statement that is NOT a significance of the battle. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: The Abyssinian army inflicted defeat on the Italian army
It led to the unification of Abyssinia

questions.enonce_markdown: The Agadir Crisis of 1911 involved which two European powers?
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1911 Germany sent the gunboat Panther to Agadir (Morocco) to challenge French control of Morocco and to ask for compensation. The crisis, the second Moroccan crisis, was between Germany and France, and it ended with a treaty in November 1911 in which Germany received part of the French Congo (Neukamerun, added to Kamerun). Britain supported France diplomatically, but the two powers at the centre of the crisis were Germany and France. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The principal architect behind the success of the British colonial policy of indirect Rule in Northern Nigeria was...
questions.corrige_markdown: Frederick Lugard, High Commissioner of Northern Nigeria from 1900 and later Governor-General, built indirect rule by governing through the Emirs and the existing Fulani-Hausa administration. Richards, Macpherson and Lyttelton are known for constitutions of 1946, 1951 and 1954, not for creating indirect rule. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Under the French policy of assimilation, they considered Africans as being in "father-son" relationship. This aspect of assimilation was referred to as...
questions.corrige_markdown: In the French view the colonial power was the 'father' who guided and civilised the African 'child': this attitude is paternalism. 'Prestation' was the labour tax paid by Africans, differentiation is not the name of this aspect, and association was the policy that replaced assimilation and respected local institutions. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Kenya was a classical example of a white settler colony. This statement is true because...

*Options as printed:* A) British nationals in Kenya were in the majority   B) British nationals settled in Kenya with no intention to ever leave.   C) British nationals dominated the economy of Kenya   D) The administrative and legislative councils were dominated by the British.
questions.corrige_markdown:
A white settler colony is one where European settlers came to live permanently, took the best land (the 'White Highlands' of Kenya) and dominated its economy and politics. Option A is false (the settlers were a small minority, a few tens of thousands among millions of Africans), but options B, C and D all describe real features of settler Kenya, so the printed question has no single clear key and is left open. The defining feature is B: settlers came to stay.

**Intended answer: B (British nationals settled in Kenya with no intention to ever leave).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A significant contribution made by Africans in the Victory of the Allied powers in the First World War was...
questions.corrige_markdown: Africa did not manufacture machine guns, warships or aircraft. Its contribution was soldiers and carriers (not listed here) and raw materials (rubber, palm oil and kernels, cocoa, copper and food) that fed the Allied war effort. **Answer: D.**
themes: impact of world war one on africa

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following African territories did NOT constitute a battle ground during the first world war?
questions.corrige_markdown: Fighting took place in Togoland (invaded in August 1914 by British and French forces), in Cameroon, in German South West Africa and in German East Africa, which is Tanganyika (the name used after the war); options B and D therefore name the same battleground. The Gold Coast supplied troops that fought in Togoland and other theatres, but it was not itself a theatre of war. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify from the list below a prominent leader of an African country who temporarily lost his throne in 1936 but regained it in 1941 as a result of the outbreak of the Second World War.
questions.corrige_markdown: Italy invaded Ethiopia in October 1935 and took Addis Ababa in May 1936, forcing Emperor Haile Selassie into exile. When Italy entered the Second World War, British and Ethiopian forces drove the Italians out and he returned to his capital in May 1941. Menelik II died in 1913, Mengistu Haile Mariam ruled from 1974 to 1991, and Mohammed V was the King of Morocco. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the nationalist who championed the formation of RDA in French West Africa in 1946.
questions.corrige_markdown: The African Democratic Rally (RDA) was founded at Bamako in October 1946, and its main founder and first president was the Ivorian Felix Houphouet-Boigny. Sekou Toure and Modibo Keita were important members of its Guinean and Sudanese sections, and Leopold Senghor of Senegal followed a different political line (he did not found the RDA). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Select from the list below an African nationalist who was associated with NCNC leadership in the decolonisation of Nigeria
questions.corrige_markdown: The National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC), created in 1944, was led by Herbert Macaulay and then by Nnamdi Azikiwe, who became its best known leader and later the first President of Nigeria. Awolowo led the Action Group and Tafawa Balewa belonged to the Northern People's Congress. Eyo Ita was also a nationalist of the early NCNC years, but Azikiwe is the leader linked to the party. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The nationalist movement that resisted British colonial rule and greatly contributed to the attainment of independence for Kenya was...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Mau Mau rising (about 1952-1960), mostly of Kikuyu fighters, challenged British rule and the loss of land, forced the British to reform, and helped lead to Kenya's independence in December 1963. The ANC belongs to South Africa, and the MPLA and UNITA to Angola. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: He was considered the most popular leader of Congo but overthrown in a bloody Coup by the Belgian Colonial master in the 1960s. His name was?
questions.corrige_markdown: Patrice Lumumba, first Prime Minister of the independent Congo (June 1960), was dismissed and overthrown in September 1960 in the crisis in which Belgium and the Katanga secession played a part, and he was killed in January 1961. Tshombe led the Katanga secession, Kasavubu was the first President, and Mobutu took power later. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The Nigeria leader who led loyal state forces against the Biafran sessessionists in 1966 was...
questions.corrige_markdown: General Yakubu Gowon, Head of State of Nigeria from July 1966, led the federal forces against the Biafran secession of Lieutenant-Colonel Ojukwu in the civil war of 1967-1970 (the secession was declared in 1967, not in 1966 as printed). General Ironsi had been killed in July 1966, and Ojukwu was the Biafran leader. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In which country and in what year did the first summit of the African Union take place?
questions.corrige_markdown: The African Union replaced the OAU and was launched in Durban, South Africa, in July 2002, with the first AU summit held there. The Sirte summit of Libya (1999 and 2001) belonged to the transition, and Addis Ababa in Ethiopia is the headquarters, not the place of the first summit. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The industrialisation of Europe in the 19th Century contributed to the outbreak of the First World War in all of the following ways EXCEPT...
questions.corrige_markdown: Industrialisation produced more goods than Europe could sell, so powers competed for markets and colonies (A), they sought raw materials in colonies and clashed (B), and modern industry made weapons and navies for the arms race (C). Colonial conferences such as the Berlin Conference were attempts to settle colonial claims peacefully and are not a way in which industrialisation led to the war. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Mass production resulting to colonial clashes.
Search for raw materials resulting to colonial rivalry
Modern technology resulting to arms race and military build ups
Colonial conferences held to discuss colonisation

questions.enonce_markdown: Which country was a member of the Dreikaiserbund but later joined the Triple Entente of 1907?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Dreikaiserbund (League of the Three Emperors) united Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia. Russia later drifted away from Germany and joined France and Britain in the Triple Entente (completed in 1907 by the Anglo-Russian agreement). Germany and Austria-Hungary stayed in the Triple Alliance, and Italy was never in the Dreikaiserbund. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The principal event that sparked up the outbreak of the First World War in 1914 was...
questions.corrige_markdown: On 28 June 1914 the Serbian nationalist Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, at Sarajevo. This was the spark. The Austrian ultimatum and the declaration of war on Serbia were consequences of it, and the Balkan Wars (1912-1913) were an earlier background. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: Austrian declaration of war on Serbia
The assassination of the Austria heir to the throne

questions.enonce_markdown: The name of the Country whose entering into First World War on the Allied side greatly contributed to the defeat of the central powers was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The United States entered the war on the Allied side in April 1917, bringing fresh troops, money and supplies when the Allies were tired, and this helped to defeat the Central Powers in 1918. Russia left the war in 1917, and France and Britain had been in the war since 1914. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The name of the European leader who represented France in the Paris Peace Treaty of 1919 was ...
questions.corrige_markdown: France was represented at the Paris Peace Conference by its Prime Minister Georges Clemenceau, who wanted a harsh peace for Germany. Orlando represented Italy, Wilson the United States and Lloyd George Britain. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the event which caused the British to abandon the Policy of Appeasement
questions.corrige_markdown: Britain and France had accepted Hitler's demands (Rhineland, Anschluss, Sudetenland at Munich in 1938). When Germany occupied the rest of Czechoslovakia in March 1939, in breach of the Munich agreement, Britain concluded that Hitler could not be trusted and abandoned appeasement, giving a guarantee to Poland. The attack on Poland in September 1939 led to the declaration of war, but the policy had been dropped before. The Manchuria and Abyssinia invasions (1931 and 1935) took place while appeasement was still being applied. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: The German attack on Poland in 1939

questions.enonce_markdown: "An ideological war fought between the East and West after the Second World War" was referred to as ...
questions.corrige_markdown: The Cold War was the struggle of ideas, propaganda and rivalry without direct fighting between the capitalist West (led by the USA) and the communist East (led by the USSR) after 1945. Peaceful coexistence and detente were policies to reduce tension, and non-alignment was the position of states that joined neither bloc. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: In what year did the League of Nations go operational?
questions.corrige_markdown: The Covenant of the League was written at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919 and was part of the Treaty of Versailles, but the League became operational in January 1920 when the Treaty came into force, with its first Council meeting in the same month. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Identify the UN organ in charge of the administrative functions of the organisation.
questions.corrige_markdown: The Secretariat, headed by the Secretary-General, runs the day-to-day administration of the UN. The General Assembly debates and votes, the Security Council deals with peace and security, and the International Court of Justice settles legal disputes between states. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Movement of people across international frontiers resulting from crises and political instability give rise to a phenomenon referred to as ...

*Options as printed:* A) Terrorism   B) Refugeeism   C) International migration   D) Tourism
questions.corrige_markdown:
People who flee across a border because of war, persecution or political instability are refugees, and the phenomenon is called refugeeism (the refugee problem). Terrorism and tourism have nothing to do with it, and international migration is the wider name for any movement across frontiers, including for work or study, so the printed question is left open.

**Intended answer: B (Refugeeism).**
